pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Describe the token bucket your limiter implements, and why the clock is injected rather than read from `time.Now`.
expected_points: each key has a bucket of at most burst tokens refilling at rate per second; a request spends one
burst absorbs a legitimate short spike while the long-run average stays at rate
the balance and its timestamp are stored and refill is computed on read — no goroutine per client
an injected clock makes the tests deterministic instead of sleeping, which matters under -race
the bucket map is shared across request goroutines so it needs a mutex

questions.prompt: You ship this limiter set to 100 requests/second and run four replicas. What is the real limit, and what else about this limiter is weaker than it looks?
expected_points: per-instance, so four replicas allow roughly 400/s — global limiting needs shared state or a gateway
the key is only as good as what you can trust: RemoteAddr is shared by NAT, X-Forwarded-For is client-controlled
the bucket map grows per distinct key, so idle buckets must be evicted or the map is itself a DoS
eviction must not be faster than a full refill or it hands the client a fresh bucket

questions.prompt: What does CORS actually protect, what is a preflight request asking, and why is `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials a bug?
expected_points: the same-origin policy stops a page reading a cross-origin response; CORS is how the API opts into letting it
it is enforced by the browser, so it is not access control — curl ignores it and the handler still runs
a preflight is OPTIONS + Access-Control-Request-Method/-Headers asking permission before a non-simple request
wildcard plus credentials would let any site act as the logged-in user; browsers refuse it, and reflecting Origin is worse
Vary: Origin is required whenever the response depends on the origin, or a cache mixes them up

questions.prompt: Which security response headers earn their place on a JSON API, and what attack does each one stop? Name one you deliberately do not send.
expected_points: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops the browser guessing a type and executing a response as HTML
CSP with default-src 'none' and frame-ancestors 'none' — nothing loads, nobody frames it
HSTS stops a plaintext downgrade, and is only meaningful (and only honoured) over TLS
X-XSS-Protection is dead and was itself a vulnerability; X-Frame-Options is redundant next to frame-ancestors
being able to justify each header is the point — an unexplained header is a liability

questions.prompt: Walk through what `DecodeJSON` does to a request body, in order, and which status code each failure earns.
expected_points: reject a Content-Type that is not application/json with 415
wrap the body in http.MaxBytesReader — an unbounded body is a memory DoS — and answer 413
DisallowUnknownFields so a typo or a smuggled field is a 400, not a silent success
check there is exactly one JSON value; trailing data is a 400
malformed is 400, semantically invalid is 422, with field-level errors naming every failing field

questions.prompt: A colleague says boundary validation makes parameterized queries unnecessary. Answer them.
expected_points: validation answers 'is this acceptable to my domain'; injection is a property of the sink's language
each sink has its own rule: SQL placeholders, contextual HTML encoding, shell quoting
blocklisting characters breaks legitimate data (O'Brien) and still misses encodings
accept the character, escape it where it is used; the two are complements, not substitutes

questions.prompt: Name the server timeouts and what each one prevents, then explain why WriteTimeout must be larger than your handler timeout.
expected_points: ReadHeaderTimeout (slow headers), ReadTimeout (slow body), WriteTimeout (client stops reading), IdleTimeout (parked keep-alives)
they all default to zero, which means no limit
TimeoutHandler answers 503 but cannot kill the handler goroutine, so contexts must be checked downward
if WriteTimeout is smaller the connection dies before the 503 explaining the failure can be sent

questions.prompt: Defend your middleware order. What breaks if CORS moves inside the rate limiter, and what breaks if the rate limiter moves inside the decoder?
expected_points: a 429 without CORS headers is unreadable to the browser — the frontend sees 'network error' instead of your status
rate limiting inside parsing means a refused client still made you read a body and decode it
security headers outermost so rejections carry them too
the trade-off taken: preflights answered by CORS bypass the limiter, which is acceptable for small bodyless requests
